questions.explain: The chapter advises sizing text columns deliberately — NVARCHAR(MAX) only when data genuinely has no bound — because it disables indexing optimizations and inflates storage.
options: It disables certain indexing optimizations, inflates storage, and pushes large values off-row into LOB allocation units
It makes the column case-insensitive
It forces the database into Read Uncommitted
It prevents JSON functions from working on the column
questions.q: The chapter calls NVARCHAR(MAX) for every text column a common production mistake. Why?

questions.explain: The chapter says a timestamp without its offset is ambiguous once it leaves the server that wrote it, so DATETIMEOFFSET is right across time zones; DATETIME2 beats legacy DATETIME on precision and range and should be the default.
options: DATETIMEOFFSET uses less storage than DATETIME2
DATETIMEOFFSET carries the UTC offset with the value, while DATETIME2 improves precision and range over legacy DATETIME
DATETIMEOFFSET automatically converts values to local server time
DATETIME2 stores values in UTC by default
questions.q: Why does the chapter recommend DATETIMEOFFSET for timestamps that cross time zones, and DATETIME2 as the default otherwise?

questions.explain: Because SQL uses three-valued logic, one NULL makes NOT IN UNKNOWN for every row, so the query silently returns no data and no error — the chapter recommends NOT EXISTS instead.
options: It returns an error
The NULL rows are silently skipped
The entire NOT IN expression evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row, so the query returns zero results
It behaves exactly like NOT EXISTS
questions.q: If a subquery used with NOT IN returns even one NULL value, what happens to the outer query?

questions.explain: The chapter warns that by default SQL Server does not abort an entire transaction on a statement error, so a later COMMIT could commit partial work; SET XACT_ABORT ON prevents that.
options: It improves query performance by disabling locking
It allows partial commits to succeed faster
It makes any statement error terminate the batch and roll back the transaction instead of leaving it open with locks held
It automatically enables RCSI for the session
questions.q: Why does the chapter recommend SET XACT_ABORT ON inside explicit transactions in SQL Server?

questions.explain: The chapter describes schema-level grants as a powerful RBAC pattern: grant at the schema level and new objects inherit the right permissions automatically.
options: It grants access to all current and future objects within that schema
It grants SELECT on every table in every database on the instance
It only applies to objects that exist at grant time
It requires the grantee to be a server-level login
questions.q: In SQL Server's object hierarchy, what is the practical effect of granting SELECT on a schema?
